title: Boundary scan
summary: The original purpose of JTAG: testing the **solder joints and wires** of a printed circuit board without probes. Every pin of a chip gets a boundary-scan cell; together they let the tester drive and observe the board's nets.
objectives: Describe a boundary-scan cell and its modes.
Explain how EXTEST finds opens and shorts between chips.
Compute the number of patterns for a counting-sequence interconnect test.
Explain the role of the BSDL file.

blocks.md: A **boundary-scan cell** sits between a pin and the chip's core. It has a **capture/shift** flip-flop, an **update** latch and a mux. All cells of a chip form the **boundary-scan register** (BSR).

rows: transparent: core ↔ pin, the chip works normally
captures the pin value **without** disturbing operation
loads values into the update latches, ready for EXTEST
output pins are driven from the update latches; input pins are captured
blocks.caption: Modes of a boundary-scan cell

steps.title: Normal operation
steps.md: Two chips connected by four nets. In normal mode the boundary-scan cells are transparent.

steps.title: Drive
steps.md: With **EXTEST**, chip A drives a pattern — 1 0 1 0 — from its boundary-scan cells onto the nets.

steps.title: Capture and compare
steps.md: Chip B captures the nets in its cells. The tester shifts the whole chain out and compares: everything matches.

steps.title: A short
steps.md: Solder bridges nets 2 and 3. The driver of net 2 (0) wins in this example, so chip B reads **0** on net 3 instead of 1 — the short is found.

steps.title: An open
steps.md: Net 4 is not soldered. Chip B's input floats (here to 1) instead of following the driven 0 — the open is found.

blocks.title: Why it changed board test
blocks.md: Before boundary scan, boards were tested with a **bed of nails** — a fixture with a probe for every net. Fine-pitch packages such as BGAs hide their pins under the chip, so probes cannot reach them. Boundary scan tests the same nets through four wires.

Give every net a **unique binary code** and apply the codes bit by bit, one pattern per bit. A short makes two nets read the same, an open makes a net read a constant — both break the codes. Codes of all 0s and all 1s are not used (a stuck net would look like them), so for N nets:

> number of patterns = ⌈log₂(N + 2)⌉

blocks.caption: The counting-sequence test grows only with log N

subsections.title: BSDL: describing a chip's boundary scan

blocks.md: Test tools need to know each chip's IR length, instruction codes, IDCODE and the order of its boundary-scan cells. This comes in a **BSDL** file (Boundary Scan Description Language), written in a subset of VHDL and supplied by the chip vendor. A tool combines the BSDL files with the board netlist and generates the board test automatically.
